hints.junior: Animating top looked fine with three items, then visibly stuttered with thirty — the browser has to recalculate layout for everything, every frame.
hints.mid: Any layout-affecting property (top, left, width, margin) forces a full recalculation each animation frame — transform and opacity don't.
hints.staff: The fix isn't animating faster — it's letting layout jump instantly and faking the animation entirely with a transform, which is what FLIP does.

hints.junior: Shuffle a few times in each mode — the difference gets clearer as more items reorder at once.
hints.mid: The broken mode animates top/left directly; the fixed mode measures positions before and after, then animates only a transform.
hints.staff: Open DevTools Performance while shuffling — the broken mode shows recurring Layout work per frame the fixed mode simply doesn't have.

hints.junior: First: measure position. Last: let the DOM jump there instantly. Invert: fake it back with a transform. Play: remove the transform and let it transition.
hints.mid: dx/dy between First and Last become a transform with no transition, then next frame that transform is removed with a transition applied.
hints.staff: This works because transform on a composited layer skips main-thread layout and paint entirely — the technique changes which pipeline stage does the work.

hints.junior: FLIP isn't a general animation library — items entering or leaving the list need separate handling, it only covers items that persist and move.
hints.mid: Elements must exist in the DOM at both First and Last for the measurement to work — new/removed items need their own enter/exit logic.
hints.staff: Batch all First measurements before mutating the DOM and all Last measurements after — interleaving reads and writes causes layout thrashing.

sections.junior: Hey! Today's case is about a list-reorder animation that looked fine with a few items and visibly stuttered once there were dozens.
The fix is the FLIP technique — measure the starting position, let the DOM jump straight to the end position, then fake the animation with a cheap transform instead of an expensive layout property.
Shuffle the list in both modes and watch how each one holds up as more items move at once.
Don't animate top or left for a list reorder. Measure before and after, then animate only a transform — same visual result, none of the layout cost.
